0 · Overview & architecture

This document is the engineering specification for ODYSSEY: a seamless space-to-surface exploration sim with Kerbal-grade orbital mechanics and No Man's Sky-grade procedural planetary detail. The playable build in this file is a working reference implementation in WebGL — every system described below exists here in miniature, so you can read the spec and the running code side by side.

The four hard problems

Everything else in a game like this is ordinary engineering. These four are not, and every architectural decision below exists to serve one of them:

ProblemWhy it breaks naïve enginesSolution adopted
PrecisionA float32 has 24 bits of mantissa. At Saturn (1.4e12 m) it resolves ~130 km. Vertices jitter, physics explodes.Floating origin + double-precision simulation state. The camera is pinned to (0,0,0); the universe is translated around it in doubles before anything reaches the GPU.
Depth rangeNear 0.1 m and far 1e13 m cannot coexist in a 24-bit fixed-point depth buffer.Logarithmic depth (WebGL / older HW) or reversed-Z float depth (DX12/Vulkan, preferred in UE5). Fallback: multi-frustum layered rendering.
Detail at all scalesYou cannot author or stream a 6371 km sphere at 1 m resolution — that is 5e14 texels.Everything is a function. A CDLOD cube-sphere quadtree evaluates the same noise field at whatever frequency the current LOD needs.
Two authoritiesTerrain is generated on the GPU but collision must be queried on the CPU.One bit-exact integer hash shared by both implementations. Never frac(sin(dot(p,k))*43758.5) — it diverges between vendors and between CPU and GPU.

Layer diagram

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PRESENTATION      HDRP volumes · post stack · UI (UI Toolkit)        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ RENDER            PlanetRenderer · AtmosphereRenderer · VFXDirector  │
│                   (all consume RenderOrigin, never world positions)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ SCALE             FloatingOriginManager  ·  ScaleContext             │
│                   double3 world  ->  float3 render                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ SIMULATION        GravitySystem · OrbitalPropagator · VesselPhysics  │
│                   · Aerodynamics · ThermalModel · ResourceSystem     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ GENERATION        TerrainField (shared HLSL+C#) · BiomeField         │
│                   · ScatterField · CloudField                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ DATA              SystemDefinition (ScriptableObject) · BodyDef      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The single most important rule: no gameplay or rendering code is allowed to see an absolute world coordinate as a float. Simulation state is double3. Anything crossing into rendering goes through ScaleContext.ToRender(double3) → float3, which subtracts the current origin. If you break this rule once, you will spend a week hunting a "mysterious jitter at Jupiter".

Update order (critical)

  1. FixedUpdate — gravity, propagation, vessel rigidbody integration (all in doubles).
  2. Update — input, autopilot, systems (fuel/O2/power/thermal).
  3. LateUpdate (early) — camera solve → FloatingOriginManager.Rebase(cameraWorld).
  4. LateUpdate (late) — every renderable pulls its render transform from the new origin. Quadtree LOD selection runs here using camera-local coordinates.
  5. onPreRender — atmosphere uniforms, corner-ray basis, VFX parameter push.

Rebasing before renderable updates in the same frame is what prevents the one-frame swim you see in most floating-origin implementations.

1 · Project folder structure

Unity 2022.3 LTS or Unity 6, HDRP. Assembly definitions are listed because they are what keeps compile times sane once the terrain system grows — Odyssey.Generation must never reference Odyssey.Gameplay.

Why one scene? Additive scene loading fights floating origin — every loaded scene's transforms must be rebased too. Keep a single gameplay scene and stream data (patches, scatter, props) rather than scenes.

2 · Orbital physics & gravity

The design follows KSP's proven split: celestial bodies are on rails (analytic Kepler about their parent) and only vessels are integrated. This is not a shortcut — it is the only way to make a 100 000× time warp stable. An n-body integrator running the whole system will drift Mercury out of its orbit in a few simulated decades.

CelestialBody.cs

OrbitalPropagator.cs — universal variable formulation

One code path handles ellipse, parabola and hyperbola. This is the routine that makes "warp to periapsis" instant and exact; it is also what draws the orbit line and predicts SOI transitions.

GravitySystem.cs — what the vessel actually feels

Vessels get true summed n-body gravity from every body. It is ~20 bodies, so the cost is irrelevant, and you get Lagrange points, slingshots and mascon perturbations for free.

Time warp state machine

Two integration modes, switched by a predicate. Getting this predicate right is most of the "feel" of a KSP-like game:

ModeConditionMethod
Integratedwarp ≤ 10 or engines lit or ρ > 0 or on the ground Symplectic / velocity-Verlet substeps, h ≤ 8 ms in atmosphere, h ≤ 40 ms in vacuum.
On railseverything else Propagate() about the SOI body across the whole frame's simulated dt. Exact, O(1) in warp factor.

Clamp warp automatically when the predicate flips (entering atmosphere, lighting engines) and tell the player why — silently dropping warp is the number one usability complaint in this genre.

3 · Floating origin & scale management

Unity's Transform is float3. That is non-negotiable, so the world must come to the camera. Every frame, after the camera has been solved but before any renderable updates, the origin is re-anchored on the camera and every registered object recomputes its render transform from its authoritative double3.

ScaleContext.cs + FloatingOriginManager.cs

Things that break if you get this wrong

  • Particles. World-space particle systems keep absolute positions. Either simulate them in local space, or shift every live particle by -OriginDelta each frame (the reference implementation in this file does the latter — see ParticleSys.update).
  • Trails and ribbons. Same problem, same fix. In VFX Graph, add a global _OriginDelta and subtract it in an Update block.
  • Physics. Unity's Rigidbody is float. Run your own double integrator for the vessel and drive a kinematic rigidbody for collision queries only — never let PhysX own the state.
  • Audio. AudioSource positions are floats relative to the listener; since the listener sits at the origin, this is automatically correct once you rebase.
  • Shadow cascades. The directional light must be repositioned near the player each frame; a light at the Sun's real position produces a shadow frustum 1.5e11 m long.

Rebase cadence

Rebasing every frame is the simplest and — counter-intuitively — the cheapest option, because the subtraction is a handful of doubles per object. Threshold-based rebasing (only when the camera moves > 1 km) saves nothing measurable and introduces a visible pop when it finally triggers. Rebase every frame.

Depth

Two-camera deep sky: render bodies further than ~1e9 m with a second camera whose projection maps them onto a unit shell — position them at normalize(worldDir) * shellRadius and scale by trueRadius/trueDistance * shellRadius. Angular size is preserved exactly, depth precision is trivial, and the seam is invisible because nothing occludes at that range except other distant bodies.

4 · Procedural planet system

A CDLOD cube-sphere quadtree. Six root faces; each node subdivides into four when its projected size exceeds the target. The mesh is a fixed grid (a single shared index buffer for every patch in the game); only the vertex data differs.

The patch contract

AttributeProduced byWhy
positionOSCPU, in doubles, relative to the patch centre A point on a 6371 km sphere needs 23 bits just for the integer part. Subtracting the patch centre on the CPU brings it back to metres.
unitDirCPU (normalised cube point) This is the noise domain. float32 gives ~6e-8 relative precision, which caps usable noise frequency at about R/6 m features — plenty.
skirtCPU flag on the outer ring Pushed down by ~3 % of the patch size in the vertex shader. Hides LOD cracks without any neighbour-stitching bookkeeping.
height, normal, splatGPURecomputed every frame in the vertex shader, or baked once into a patch texture on lower-end targets.

PlanetQuadTree.cs

Budgets that matter

  • Generation budget: 3–8 patches per frame. Never generate on demand in the same frame a node splits; queue it and keep the parent visible. A 200 ms hitch while landing is far worse than a slightly coarse patch for three frames.
  • Pooling: allocate Mesh + GraphicsBuffer objects once into a pool sized for your worst case (~600 patches) and recycle. GC spikes are the usual cause of "stutter on approach".
  • Readback: if you generate on the GPU and need CPU collision, do not AsyncGPUReadback every patch — that is the classic 4-frame-latency trap. Evaluate the CPU mirror of the noise on demand, at exactly the handful of points you need (gear contacts, footsteps, scatter placement).

Scatter (the No Man's Sky "density" trick)

Rocks, flora and debris are not stored. For each leaf patch at level ≥ N, a compute shader lays a jittered grid over the patch, evaluates BiomeField at each point, rejects by density, samples TerrainField for the height and normal, and appends an instance transform to an AppendStructuredBuffer. Draw with Graphics.RenderMeshIndirect. Costs one dispatch per patch creation and zero per frame.

5 · Terrain compute shader & the shared noise contract

This is the file that must be bit-identical to its C# twin. Everything else in the project can drift a little; this cannot, or your landing gear will float or sink.

Shaders/Include/NoiseHash.hlsl

Shaders/Include/TerrainField.hlsl

Shaders/Compute/PatchGenerate.compute

Cost sanity check. 300 visible patches × 33² vertices × 3 height evaluations × ~40 noise octaves ≈ 40 M noise samples per frame. At ~50 ALU each that is ~2 TFLOP/s of headroom on a modern discrete GPU — comfortable. If you bake to patch textures instead, it drops to once per patch creation, at the cost of ~35 KB of VRAM per patch.

6 · Ship controller

One controller, two regimes, blended by dynamic pressure rather than switched. A hard mode switch at the Kármán line feels terrible; crossfading on q feels like an aircraft that happens to also be a spacecraft.

ShipController.cs

AutopilotSAS.cs — the KSP-feel autopilot

7 · Aerodynamics, heating & the re-entry sequence

Angle of attack is computed in the body frame against the co-rotating atmosphere. Both of those matter: the first gives you banked turns for free, the second is why launching eastward is cheaper.

AerodynamicsModel.cs

ThermalModel.cs

The re-entry sequence — beat by beat

The spectacle is a sequence, not an effect. Drive all of it from ReentryIntensity and altitude so it self-schedules:

PhaseTrigger (Earth)What fires
Interfacealt < 120 km, ρ > 1e-7 HUD "ENTRY INTERFACE" callout; VOL_Reentry volume starts blending; low-frequency rumble bed fades in; autopilot suggests surface-retrograde.
IonisationskinT > 900 K Plasma sheath mesh enables ahead of the vessel along the relative wind, not the nose; trailing spark VFX; camera shake ramps; chromatic aberration + warm grade climb with intensity.
Peak heatingρ·v³ maximum, ~60 km Sheath goes white-blue at the stagnation point; radio blackout (UI static, comms disabled); g-load peaks 4–8 g; heat haze distortion at maximum.
DecelerationM < 5 Plasma fades to a glowing wake; airframe buffet (high-frequency shake); control surfaces gain authority — the vessel starts flying instead of falling.
Approachalt < 10 km Terrain LOD has long since reached full depth; wind audio dominant; gear callout; landing lights auto-on below 3 km.
Touchdowngear contact Suspension compresses over ~0.4 m; dust kicked radially from each contact, tinted by the biome albedo; engine audio cuts to spool-down; a short settle wobble; "LANDED" state latches.
Orient the plasma to the airflow, never to the hull. The single most common mistake is parenting the sheath to the ship's nose. Place it along normalize(velocity − atmosphereVelocity); when the player yaws during entry, the sheath stays on the windward side and the shot instantly reads as real.

8 · Landing gear & touchdown

Three independent spring-dampers raycast against the CPU terrain field, not against a collider. There is no mesh collider on a procedural planet — building one would defeat the whole architecture.

Dust & downwash

  • Contact dust — a radial burst at each foot, speed ∝ impact velocity, colour sampled from the biome albedo so Mars kicks ochre and Luna kicks grey. Half-life ~2 s, gravity-affected, and on an airless body it must fall ballistically with no drag — that single detail is what makes the Moon read as the Moon.
  • Engine downwash — while throttle > 4 % and radar altitude < 120 m, spawn from the projected ground point with outward radial velocity ∝ throttle. Add a decal ring that darkens as it scours.
  • In atmosphere, add a rolling ground-effect torus; in vacuum, particles must travel much further before falling.

9 · Wormhole creation & travel

A four-phase sequencer. The lensing is screen-space; the throat is geometry; the transit is a tube the camera lives inside. Nothing here needs a real GR integrator — it needs to read as one.

The lensing pass (HDRP CustomPass, after opaque + sky)

  • Throat mesh: a sphere whose fragment shader computes r = sqrt(1 - dot(N,V)²) as a normalised disc radius. Black core, a sharp photon ring at r≈0.90, swirling filaments outside it. Opaque in the core — a transparent "black hole" reads as a hole in the render, not as gravity.
  • Accretion disk: a ring mesh billboarded to the viewer, spun with angle*2 − time*(3.2 − t*2.2) so the inner edge leads. Multiply by a Doppler term 0.55 + 0.75·sin(θ + φ) — one limb brighter and bluer is the single cue that sells relativistic rotation.
  • Tunnel: an inverted cylinder, depthTest off, parented to the camera rotation. Scroll two fbm layers at different rates and add a bright exit glow that ramps in the last third. That glow doing the "approaching the exit" work is why the transit needs no camera dolly.

10 · Shader & VFX recipes

10.1 Atmosphere — single-scattering raymarch

Screen-space pass, reading the depth buffer, for the body you are closest to; a cheap back-face shell for every other body. Nishita/Bruneton single scattering with Rayleigh + Mie is the right default: it gives you a blue zenith, an orange sunset, a blue limb from orbit and correct aerial perspective from one integral, with no LUT authoring.

BodyβRayleigh (per m, RGB)HrCharacter
Earth5.8e-6, 13.5e-6, 33.1e-68500 mBlue zenith, red sunset
Mars1.95e-5, 1.35e-5, 9.0e-611100 mButterscotch sky, blue sunset — invert the ratio and it falls out automatically
Venus9.0e-6, 12e-6, 7e-6 ×2.115900 mOpaque yellow soup; raise βMie hard
Titan1.4e-5, 1.1e-5, 6e-6 ×1.921000 mOrange haze, extreme Mie, huge scale height

10.2 Volumetric clouds

  • Raymarch a spherical slab between R+bottom and R+top, in the planet's local frame, with the ray origin analytically clipped — do not rely on the mesh surface.
  • Density = low-frequency fbm for coverage, minus high-frequency detail for erosion, times a vertical profile (smoothstep(0,0.20,h) · (1−smoothstep(0.52,1,h))) that gives flat bottoms and wispy tops.
  • Lighting: 2–3 samples toward the sun, Beer's law exp(−τ), plus a powder term 1−exp(−2σΔ) that restores the dark edges Beer alone loses.
  • Always include the planet-shadow test in the light march, or the night side glows.
  • Render at half resolution with a Bayer/blue-noise offset and a temporal reprojection — clouds are the one effect where TAA-style upsampling is nearly free quality.

10.3 Terrain surface

  • Splatting by height, slope, latitude and a moisture field. Four weights packed into one float4, generated in the same compute pass as the positions.
  • Triplanar only on slopes above ~35° — it is twice the samples, so gate it.
  • Parallax occlusion on the two dominant layers within ~40 m of the camera; disable beyond that (the silhouette benefit disappears and it costs 16–32 taps).
  • Micro-detail normals sampled in patch-local coordinates. Absolute planet coordinates quantise in float32; patch-local metres do not. Blend the detail in over the last two LOD levels.
  • Distance-blend the albedo toward the macro biome colour past ~2 km so tiling never becomes visible from orbit.

10.4 Ocean

Reuse the terrain quadtree and clamp the displacement to sea level — a separate water quadtree is double the LOD bookkeeping for no gain. Sum 4–6 Gerstner waves for the near field, switch to a scrolling normal-map pair beyond ~500 m. Depth-based absorption (Beer's law on seaLevel − terrainHeight), a Schlick fresnel toward the sky colour, and a sharp sun glint (specular exponent ~900). Screen-space reflections only in the last 200 m; below that nobody looks.

10.5 Thruster plumes

  • Nested cones, additive, DoubleSide, depth-write off: a white-hot core cone inside a wider translucent one. The rim term pow(1−|dot(N,V)|, 1.4) is what makes a flat cone read as a volume.
  • Vacuum vs. atmosphere: in vacuum the plume is long, dim, wide and has no shock diamonds; at sea level it is short, bright, tight, with diamonds 0.55 + 0.45·sin(t·30 − time·4). Crossfade on ambient pressure.
  • A real PointLight at the nozzle, intensity ∝ throttle, colour shifting from blue (vacuum) to orange (sea level). It is the single cheapest thing that makes engines feel powerful.
  • Heat haze: a separate quad behind the plume that samples the colour buffer with a UV offset driven by scrolling noise. In HDRP this is a CustomPass after transparents (or a Distortion-mode shader).

10.6 Re-entry plasma

  • Bow shock = an ellipsoid ahead of the vessel, oriented to the relative wind, fresnel alpha, flow-noise scrolling backwards along the local −Z.
  • Temperature ramp: deep orange → yellow-white → blue-white at the stagnation point. Drive the mix with saturate((skinT − 900)/1400), which is already tracked by the thermal model.
  • A long tapered wake cone behind the vessel, 10–20× the hull length, plus GPU sparks advected backwards with turbulence.
  • Post: chromatic aberration ∝ intensity, warm tint, vignette pulse, and camera shake with a high-frequency component (buffet) layered on a low-frequency one (rumble).

10.7 Post stack (HDRP volume order)

  1. Exposure — physical camera, manual with altitude-driven overrides. Automatic exposure will hunt violently when a bright limb crosses the frame.
  2. Bloom — progressive down/up-sample, threshold just above 1.0 in HDR, ~0.4 intensity. Low threshold + high intensity looks cheap; the reverse looks expensive.
  3. Lens flare — data-driven, occlusion-tested analytically against body spheres (never a depth query; the Sun is 1.5e11 m away).
  4. Motion blur — camera-only during normal flight; add a radial component during wormhole transit.
  5. Colour grading — one LUT per environment (space / atmosphere / re-entry), cross-faded by the same altitude driver that blends the volumes.
  6. Film grain and vignette last, both subtle. Grain at 0.03–0.04 hides banding in the atmosphere gradient better than dithering does.

11 · Ship model import & setup

Budgets

ElementTrianglesNotes
Exterior LOD0120–180 kNanite in UE5 removes this limit; in Unity keep LOD0 near 150 k and let HLOD handle the rest.
LOD1 / 2 / 345 k / 12 k / 3 kSwitch at 25 m / 120 m / 600 m screen-relative.
Cockpit interior200–300 kSeparate mesh, culled unless the first-person camera is active.
Landing gear25 kSeparate skinned or rigged hierarchy.

Texture set (per material, 4K)

  • BaseColor (sRGB) · Normal (linear, OpenGL or DirectX — be consistent) · MaskMap (HDRP packs Metallic/AO/Detail/Smoothness into RGBA — use it, it halves your sampler count) · Emissive (HDR, panel strips and windows).
  • Three material slots is the sweet spot: HullPrimary, HullTrim/Mechanical, Glass. Plus a fourth for the ablative belly if you want it to char.
  • Texel density: 512 px/m for the cockpit, 256 px/m for the exterior, 1024 px/m for anything the player's face gets within 30 cm of.

Required hierarchy

Import settings (Unity)

  • Scale factor 1.0, metres, Y-up, Z-forward. Fix it in the DCC, not the importer.
  • Read/Write off for LOD meshes (halves memory); on only for anything you raycast in C#.
  • Generate Lightmap UVs off — everything here is dynamically lit.
  • Mesh Compression off for the hero mesh; normals from the source file, tangents calculated.
  • Import Materials off. Build materials in-engine so HDRP-specific fields (MaskMap, coat mask, transmission) are authored deliberately.

Material parameters that carry the "AAA" read

  • Clearcoat 0.6–1.0 with roughness 0.02–0.05 on painted panels. This is the single biggest "expensive looking" lever on a hull.
  • Anisotropy on brushed metal trim, aligned to the panel direction.
  • Edge wear driven by a baked curvature map in the MaskMap's detail channel, not by hand painting — it survives UV changes.
  • Glass: transmission 0.92, thickness 0.35, ior 1.46, plus a faint interior grime layer. A perfectly clean canopy looks like a hole.
  • Emissive in nits (HDRP uses real units): 30–80 for panel strips, 800–2000 for nav strobes so bloom actually catches them.
If you have no art budget, build the ship parametrically — the vessel in this prototype is ~200 lines of primitive assembly (lathe fuselage, extruded delta wings, cylinder nacelles, torus rings, procedurally scattered greebles) with canvas-generated panel/rivet/wear textures. It reads convincingly at every distance and weighs nothing.

12 · Performance budget

Target: 60 fps at 1440p on an RTX 3060 / RX 6600 class GPU. Frame budget 16.6 ms.

PassBudgetControls
Terrain patches (opaque)3.5 msLOD split factor, patch grid resolution, horizon + frustum culling
Atmosphere raymarch2.0 msStep count (10/20/30/44), half-res + upsample on lower tiers
Volumetric clouds2.5 msStep count, half-res, temporal reprojection, early-out at τ>0.98
Vessel + cockpit1.5 msLODGroup, cockpit culled when not in first person
Shadows1.5 msSingle cascade fitted to the vessel (~180 m box); planets self-shadow through the normal, not shadow maps
VFX / particles1.0 msGPU-simulated; hard cap on live counts
Post stack2.0 msBloom mip count, motion blur samples
CPU simulation2.0 msBurst-compiled; substep count clamped to 48
Headroom0.6 ms

The five optimisations that actually matter

  1. Horizon culling. Roughly a third of all patches are behind the planet at low altitude. One dot product per node.
  2. Patch generation budget. Cap at 3–8 per frame and keep parents visible. This turns a 200 ms landing hitch into nothing.
  3. Bake heights to a patch texture on lower tiers instead of re-evaluating noise every vertex every frame. Trades ~35 KB VRAM per patch for ~60 % of the terrain vertex cost.
  4. GPU instancing for scatter via RenderMeshIndirect — one draw call per mesh type per patch, and zero CPU work per frame.
  5. Don't readback. CPU collision comes from the CPU noise mirror at a handful of points, never from AsyncGPUReadback of generated patches.

13 · Unreal Engine 5 variant

UE5 changes three things materially: Large World Coordinates (doubles in the core transform), Nanite (no LOD authoring for the vessel), and Lumen (real bounce light in the cockpit and off the terrain). It does not solve procedural planets for you — Nanite requires static geometry, so a runtime-generated planet still needs the quadtree.

Mapping

UnityUnreal 5Note
double3 + FloatingOriginLWC FVector + AWorldPartitionOriginShiftingLWC gives ~1 cm precision out to 88 million km. Still rebase beyond that.
PlanetQuadTree (C# + compute)UPlanetComponent (C++) driving FDynamicMeshBuilder or a custom FPrimitiveSceneProxyNanite cannot consume runtime meshes; the quadtree renders through a custom proxy.
Vessel mesh LODGroupNaniteImport the full-density model. This is the single biggest visual win UE5 offers here.
VFX GraphNiagaraGPU sim, and Niagara can read the terrain field directly via a custom Data Interface for ground-conforming dust.
HDRP CustomPassFSceneViewExtension or a post-process materialAtmosphere/lensing go here. UE's Sky Atmosphere is planet-aware and can substitute for the Rayleigh pass on the primary body.
Custom double integratorSame — bypass Chaos for the vesselUse Chaos for collision queries and debris only. Never let it own the orbital state.

Core C++ classes

World Partition warning: streaming cells assume a bounded world. For a solar system, disable World Partition on the gameplay level and stream content yourself through the quadtree — otherwise you fight two competing origin-shifting systems.

14 · Implementation roadmap

Milestone 1 — Scale & orbit (2 weeks)

  • Double-precision maths layer, ScaleContext, FloatingOriginManager.
  • Kepler propagator + on-rails bodies; Sol system data as ScriptableObjects.
  • Untextured spheres at correct scale. Free camera. Orbit line rendering.
  • Exit criterion: fly to Jupiter at 100 000× warp and return with a stable orbit and zero visible jitter. If this is not true, stop — nothing built on top will be salvageable.

Milestone 2 — Planet surface (3 weeks)

  • Shared noise hash in HLSL + C#, with a unit test asserting they agree to 1e-3 m at 10 000 random points. Write that test first.
  • Cube-sphere quadtree, skirts, patch pooling, generation budget, horizon culling.
  • Height-based splatting, ocean clamp, CPU height query.
  • Exit criterion: descend from 400 km to a hand-placed flag on the surface with no hitch > 8 ms and no visible LOD pop.

Milestone 3 — Flight model (2 weeks)

  • 6-DOF vessel, RCS, reaction wheels, SAS modes, fuel and Δv.
  • Aerodynamics, thermal model, landing gear spring-dampers.
  • Navball, orbital HUD, time-warp state machine.
  • Exit criterion: de-orbit from LEO and land on the gear, unassisted, twice in a row.

Milestone 4 — The spectacle (3 weeks)

  • Atmospheric scattering pass; volumetric clouds; ocean waves.
  • Re-entry sequencer, plasma, sparks, heat haze, post volumes.
  • Thruster plumes, landing dust, engine lights.
  • Full post stack, LUT grading per environment.
  • Exit criterion: a 60-second unedited re-entry capture that you would put in a trailer.

Milestone 5 — Wormhole & loop (2 weeks)

  • Bridge generator UI, four-phase sequencer, lensing pass, tunnel.
  • Scanner, resource survey, ship systems (O2, power, hull), damage and restore.
  • Camera director: chase / cockpit / orbital / cinematic.
  • Exit criterion: the full loop — orbit → wormhole → new world → re-entry → land → EVA → scan → launch — runs end to end without a reload.

Milestone 6 — Depth (ongoing)

  • Scatter system (rocks, flora, ruins); weather; aurora; day/night terminator effects.
  • Maneuver nodes and trajectory prediction with SOI transitions.
  • Vessel construction (the KSP half of the promise): part catalogue, attach nodes, mass and inertia solved from parts.
  • Multiple systems and interstellar bridges; base building; discovery/naming persistence.
Sequencing advice. Resist building the ship editor before Milestone 5. A construction system doubles the surface area of every physics bug you have, and it is worth nothing until flying is already good.

15 · Galaxy address space

An infinite universe is not a big database — it is a function from address to content. This section documents how No Man's Sky structures that address, why the structure is the way it is, and how this build implements it.

15.1 How No Man's Sky actually does it

Published descriptions of the game and its portal-address format agree on the following architecture:

  • The universe starts from a single 64-bit seed, run through deterministic generators. The same galaxy, with the same contents, is produced for every player.
  • Each galaxy is a fixed 4096 × 256 × 4096 grid of voxels. A voxel is a region of space, not a chunk of stored data.
  • Voxel coordinates are two's complement with the midpoint skipped: X and Z span −2047…+2047, Y spans −127…+127. (0x801 decodes to −2047, 0x7FF to +2047; the exact midpoint is not used.)
  • Each voxel holds up to 768 star systems, indexed by a SolarSystemIndex; each system holds up to 6 planets, indexed by a PlanetIndex.
  • Voxel XYZ plus the system index is internally called the GalacticAddress. The player- facing portal address is twelve glyphs laid out as [P][SSS][YY][ZZZ][XXX] — planet, system, then voxel height, width, length.
  • Systems, planets, creatures and structures are generated on first visit. Nothing exists until someone asks for it; asking is what creates it.
The insight worth stealing is not the numbers, it is that the coordinate is the seed. Because the address hashes to the content, a twelve-character string is a complete, shareable pointer to a world — and the server never has to store, sync or authorise anything about it.

15.2 The same scheme here

ConceptThis build
Grid4096 × 256 × 4096 voxels, X/Z −2047…2047, Y −127…127
Systems per voxelup to 768, set by the density field (mean ≈ 30 over occupied space)
Planets per system1–6, each with 0–3 moons
Address{ g, vx, vy, vz, ssi } + planet index
Portal string[P][SSS][YY][ZZZ][XXX], 12 glyphs over a 16-symbol alphabet
Galaxies256, each reseeding the whole field
Scale1 voxel ≈ 25 ly, so a galaxy is ≈ 102 000 ly across
Population≈ 1.3 × 1011 systems per galaxy — deliberately close to the real Milky Way's star count

Address → seed

The address is folded into the same bit-exact PCG hash the terrain uses, so one hash function drives both the shape of a mountain and the position of a star.

Portal encoding

15.3 The density field is the map

One function decides both how the galaxy looks and how many systems a voxel holds. Two logarithmic spiral arms over an exponential disc, plus a central bulge:

Because the map is drawn by sampling the same function, every point on the galaxy map is a real address. There is no separate "map data" that could disagree with the universe.

15.4 Generating a system

Draw the star first, because it sets everything downstream:

  1. Spectral class from a weighted table (M 62 %, K 18 %, G 10 %, F 5 %, A 3 %, B 1.6 %, O 0.3 %, plus rare exotics). Class fixes colour, temperature, radius and mass.
  2. Habitable zone at √luminosity AU. This single number decides which archetypes a planet may draw from, which is what makes systems feel composed rather than random — ice giants sit outside, scorched rock sits inside.
  3. Orbits by Titius–Bode-ish spacing (an+1 = an × (1.5…2.4)) so orbits never cross.
  4. Type: the probability of a gas giant rises with distance past the habitable zone.
  5. Archetype drawn from the pool its temperature band allows — lush, oceanic, overgrown, scorched, frozen, toxic, irradiated, barren, volcanic, marshland, exotic, arid. One archetype per planet, exactly as the original does it.
  6. Terrain, palette, atmosphere and clouds derived from that archetype, then jittered by the planet's own seed so two "frozen" worlds are never the same world.
Budget note: generating a system is pure arithmetic — no allocation beyond the body list, no I/O, no readback. A full system with moons builds in well under a millisecond, so warp arrival costs a frame, not a loading screen.

15.5 Swapping the live system

The only genuinely awkward part. Every subsystem holds a reference to the body list, so the lists are mutated in place rather than replaced — otherwise every module needs re-wiring on each warp:

Three things that will bite you if you skip them: cancel in-flight patch generation (a patch that lands after the swap attaches to a destroyed planet), dispose materials and their textures but not shared geometry, and re-anchor the vessel before the next physics step — its position is meaningless in the new system's frame.

16 · Touch & mobile controls

A six-degree-of-freedom spacecraft has more axes than a phone has thumbs. The job is deciding which axes get direct control, which get a momentary button, and which the autopilot should simply handle.

16.1 The allocation

InputAxisWhy
Left floating stickPitch + yawThe two axes you steer with continuously. Floating (it spawns where the thumb lands) beats a fixed stick — thumbs do not find a fixed circle without looking.
Right vertical sliderThrottleAbsolute, not incremental: you can slam to zero or full without travel time, which matters on final approach.
BURN buttonThrottle overrideMomentary 100 %, released back to the slider value. The single most-used control during landing.
⟲ ⟳ buttonsRollRoll is used in bursts, not held — a third stick axis would cost more than it returns.
▲▼ buttonsRCS translateVertical translation for hovering; the other four translation axes stay on the autopilot.
Drag anywhere elseCamera orbitA full-screen zone beneath every other control in z-order, so it only receives what nothing else claimed.
Right railMode togglesFour primary, the rest behind a "more" expander — a phone cannot show eleven buttons and still be a game.

16.2 Implementation rules that matter

  • Pointer Events, not touch events. One code path covers touch, pen and mouse, and you get pointerId for free — which is what stops two thumbs fighting over one gesture.
  • Every control owns its pointer id. Each handler ignores any event whose id is not the one it captured. Without this, sliding a second thumb onto the screen steals the stick.
  • Wrap setPointerCapture in try/catch. It throws if the pointer has already been released or is synthetic, and an uncaught throw aborts the handler before it applies the input — a control that silently does nothing.
  • Layer with z-index, then let hit-testing do the work. The camera-drag zone is a full-screen element at a lower z-index than every button; no manual bounds checks anywhere.
  • touch-action: none on every control, or the browser steals the gesture for scrolling and your stick jumps.
  • Respect the safe-area insets. env(safe-area-inset-*) on anything pinned to an edge, or the home indicator sits on your throttle.
  • Feed one control channel. Touch writes into the same ctrl / trans vectors the keyboard does, so the flight model never learns there are two input systems — and a tablet with a keyboard can use both at once.

16.3 Layout traps

Two collisions cost real debugging time here, and both are worth checking on a device before shipping: a vertically-centred action rail lands exactly on top of a bottom-anchored throttle column on a tall phone, and the navball's WebGL viewport is positioned from the bottom of the framebuffer while its DOM ring is positioned from the top — they drift apart the moment the layout changes. Drive both from one computed rectangle.

16.4 Deciding when to show them

Detection is the part that actually loses players. A screen-size test alone (min(innerWidth, innerHeight) < 1100) is wrong in both directions: it hides the touch UI on a touch laptop or a large tablet, and it can show it on a small desktop window. A hasTouch test alone is wrong too — most laptops now report a touch point. So this build uses four signals, in priority order:

SignalBeats
A stored choice (localStorage["odyssey.touch"])Everything. Guessing wrong twice in a row is worse than never guessing.
The first genuine pointerdown with pointerType of touch or penThe size heuristic. A finger is the only signal that cannot be faked by a viewport.
Touch capability and a small viewportNothing — it is the boot-time guess.
resize / orientationchange re-evaluationThe boot-time guess, but only while the player has not chosen.

And whatever the detection decides, there is always a visible way out in both directions: a toggle in the desktop button bar, and a SETUP entry on the touch rail itself. The touch stylesheet hides the desktop bar, so without that rail entry, a player who landed in touch mode by mistake would have no route back — the failure mode is not "the wrong UI", it is "no way to change the wrong UI".

17 · Galaxy morphology — how to have an unbounded number of them

A list of 256 named galaxies is a database. Replace the list with a function of the index and the count stops being a design decision: 232 galaxies, none of them stored, each one a different shape.

17.1 One field, seven morphologies

Do not write seven density functions. Write one with enough terms to cover the Hubble sequence and let the type choose the weights — that way the CPU (which decides how many systems a voxel holds) and the GPU (which draws the haze and the map sprites) can run the same formula, and they cannot drift apart:

TypeWhat the weights do
Spiral2–4 arms, sharp contrast, thin disc.
Barred spiralTwo arms plus the bar term. Tighten the bulge or the bar drowns in it.
Flocculent5–8 arms, armSharp near 1 and a high armBase: many faint arms instead of two bright ones.
EllipticalDisc weight near zero, wide bulge, thick, and squashed on one axis. Metal-poor.
LenticularDisc with no arms and a dominant bulge.
RingRing term does the work; disc almost off.
IrregularThree to five Gaussian blobs and a weak disc. No rotational symmetry at all.

17.2 Metallicity is the parameter that makes it matter

Shape alone is scenery. One extra number per galaxy — metallicity — changes what you find there, and it is free because it only reweights distributions that already existed:

  • The stellar IMF. A metal-poor elliptical runs almost entirely to red dwarfs; a metal-rich starburst has twenty times the O and B stars. Reweight STAR_CLASSES — do not add a draw, or the cheap "summary" path that replays the RNG prefix for the map stops matching the full generator.
  • The planetary archetype pool. You cannot build a rocky world out of hydrogen and helium. Below about 0.35 the pool is filtered to rock and ice; above 0.85 the lush and oceanic archetypes are entered twice.

Pin your home galaxy. Galaxy 0 contains hand-authored content — a real Solar System at a real address — so its shape is hard-coded to a four-armed barred spiral rather than left to the hash. Everything a player is told about where they started should stay true.

17.3 Drawing a galaxy in a point sprite

The universe view needs a thousand galaxies on screen, each recognisably itself. Do not use textures: run the density formula in the fragment shader of a single point sprite, with the shape parameters as vertex attributes. Squash the sprite's local coordinates by a per-galaxy inclination and you get discs seen edge-on for free. One draw call, a thousand distinct galaxies, nothing stored.

18 · Inhabitants & landmarks

A universe you can only look at goes stale in about ten minutes. The fix is not more terrain — it is things that were put there, which means a second derivation layer on top of the address space.

18.1 Species belong to regions, not planets

Rolling a species per planet gives you noise: neighbouring worlds with unrelated civilisations and no sense of territory. Roll it per super-cell instead — here a 16×8×16 block of voxels, roughly 400 light years — and a cultural sphere appears for free. Travel far enough and the architecture, the names and the disposition of everyone you meet change together, which is what makes distance feel like distance.

18.2 Landmarks have to exist in the world, not in a menu

The difference between "this planet has an observatory" as a line of text and as a thing you can land next to is entirely in whether you pinned it to the terrain. Three rules:

  • Store the direction in the body-fixed frame. A world-space direction slides across the surface as the planet rotates; you will place a base at dawn and find it in the sea by noon.
  • Stand it on the terrain normal, not the radius. On a 20° slope a radial up puts one corner of the building three metres in the air. You already have the normal — the landing gear needs it too.
  • Give it a beam. A 900 m additive cylinder costs nothing and is the only reason a player ever finds the place they were aiming at from 40 km up.

18.3 Standing on a moving world

Landmarks are why you get out of the ship. Getting out of the ship is where a heliocentric simulation quietly betrays you.

A walker integrated in world coordinates has a velocity that includes the body's own motion — Luna does 1.02 km/s around the Earth, the Earth does 30 km/s around the Sun. Take the "vertical" component of that against the local radial and you are measuring mostly orbital motion. In this build the symptom was precise and baffling: step onto the Moon, stand perfectly still, and one second later the ship is a kilometre away and refuses to let you board.

Subtracting the ground velocity before splitting into vertical and horizontal fixes the gross error. It does not fix the residual: integrating a position along the tangent of a rotating surface, once per frame, lags the surface by ½ω²r·Δt per step. On Earth that is still 36 m in a minute of standing still.

The fix is to move the whole integration into the body-fixed frame and derive world space from it, exactly as the landmarks already do:

Standing-still drift over a minute: 1032 m, then 36 m, then under 1 m.

And park the vehicle. A lander resting on broken ground creeps downhill — tens of metres a minute on a slope, which is long enough to lose your ship while you are out walking. The tempting fix, modelling static friction, makes it worse: a stiffer pad puts a larger tangential force at the foot, which torques the vehicle, which rocks it, which breaks contacts, which removes the friction. Hold the vehicle explicitly instead while nobody is aboard.

19 · Guided powered descent (auto-land)

An autopilot that plays a scripted animation breaks the first time the ground is not where the script assumed. One closed-loop law lands on a slope, in wind, at any gravity, because it never assumes anything — it reads the state and commands an acceleration.

19.1 Command an acceleration vector, not a throttle

The obvious formulation is: set throttle from a vertical-speed schedule, then tilt the nose to cancel horizontal drift. It does not work, and the reason is worth internalising. On a low-gravity world the vertical term is tiny — on the Moon a steady descent needs about 12 % throttle — so the tilt has almost no thrust behind it and the lateral authority is a tenth of a m/s². The vehicle arrives at the surface still moving sideways at 200 m/s and skids.

Command the whole acceleration instead, and read the attitude and the throttle off it:

The final division is the one everybody forgets: thrust only acts along the nose, so leaning over to brake costs you vertical thrust and you have to pay it back, or the vehicle sinks exactly when it is working hardest.

19.2 Three limits that keep it stable

LimitWhy
Tilt by altitude — 60° above 1.5 km, 26° above 300 m, 10° belowA big lean is how you kill orbital-scale sideways speed; near the ground it is how you put a landing leg through a boulder.
Tilt by dynamic pressure — scale by clamp(1 − q/4000, 0.1, 1)Angle of attack is limited by the air, not by ambition. Holding 60° at 2.5 kPa is how a lander becomes a tumbling one.
Descend no faster than you can brakeIf the horizontal speed cannot be cancelled inside the descent that is left, slow the descent: tBrake = |Δv_h| / a_h_max, tFall = h / |v_target|, and if tBrake > 0.8·tFall scale the target rate down. Hitting the ground sideways is the one failure the schedule must never allow.

And a recovery, because limits are not guarantees: above 0.8 rad/s the vehicle is not flying a guidance law, it is tumbling. Cut the throttle, hold surface-retrograde (in air) or stability assist (in vacuum), and do not steer again until the rate is back down.

19.3 Choose the ground, do not accept it

Falling wherever the trajectory happens to point puts you on a 25-degree scree slope, at rest for half a second and then sliding — and "at rest" is what gates getting out of the vehicle. Sample the height field around the projected touchdown point and steer at the flattest candidate, re-surveying as the scale changes: from 30 km a flat candidate is a 20 km plain; from 800 m it is an actual patch of ground.

Seventy height evaluations, three times per landing. It is the cheapest part of the whole system and it is the difference between landing and arriving.

19.4 When to start braking

Not at a fixed altitude — at the altitude where stopping is still possible, with margin:

The 1.40 is margin for throttle lag and for the terrain ahead being higher than the ground directly below. The horizontal term is there because sideways speed is paid for out of the same budget.

19.5 Knowing when to stop

Two failure modes here cost more debugging time than the guidance law did:

  • Contact is not touchdown. A leg grazing a ridge at 15 m/s is a skid; cutting the engine there leaves the vehicle sliding. Require an actual near-stop — ground-relative speed under about 5 m/s — before handing over to the settle phase.
  • Then stop completely. "Landed" needs the angular rate under 0.06 rad/s, and an autopilot that keeps holding an attitude command keeps the reaction wheels turning. It will hover on its own gear and never admit it has arrived. Cut throttle, switch to stability assist, set the wheel brakes, and wait.

One contact can be enough. Broken ground routinely leaves a lander balanced on a single leg with the attitude hold keeping it upright. If your "landed" test demands two contacts, the crew can never open the hatch. Test for at rest on the surface, not for a contact count.

19.6 The parts that are not guidance

ProblemResolution
A landing from orbit is twenty minutes of fallingLet the autopilot drive time warp: 50× in vacuum, 5× in thin air, 1× below ~1.2 km or whenever dynamic pressure is high. The law is closed-loop, so a coarser step costs accuracy, not stability.
Landing "somewhere" is not a destinationBias the landing-spot search toward the nearest landmark — but range-check it first. A monolith on the far side of the Moon is 1600 km away; chasing it turns a landing into an endless series of ballistic hops.
Deploy state driven by the render loopMove it into the physics step. Leg contact keys off the deploy animation, so advancing it from Update() makes whether you land on your legs or your belly depend on whether a frame was drawn.
The player wants control backAny real stick deflection disengages it, with no confirmation. An autopilot you cannot interrupt by simply flying is a trap.
Out of propellant mid-descentAbort and say so. Do not silently keep thrusting — that is the bug that makes players distrust every other system.

20 · This prototype's mapping

The build you are flying implements the spec above in a single HTML file with no external assets. If you are porting to Unity or Unreal, these are the pieces to read first:

Spec sectionIn this file
Floating originorigin, renderPos(), updateCamera() — the camera is pinned to (0,0,0) and originDelta is fed to the particle systems.
Orbital mechanicspropagateUV() (universal variable), elementsToState(), stateToElements(), gravityAt(), dominantBody().
Shared noise contractGLSL_NOISE (GPU) and NZ (CPU) — the same PCG integer hash, plus GLSL_TERRAIN / terrainHeightJS().
QuadtreeQNode, buildPatchGeometry(), PlanetView.update(), horizonCull().
AtmosphereatmoMat (screen-space raymarch reading the log-depth buffer) and GLOW_FRAG (cheap shell for distant bodies).
CloudsCLOUD_FRAG — slab raymarch with Beer-powder lighting and a planet-shadow test.
Flight modelaeroAndThrust(), attitudeControl(), integrate() (Euler's equation with the gyroscopic term), stepPhysics().
LandinggearPhysics() — three spring-dampers against the CPU noise field.
Galaxy morphologygalaxyShape(), galaxyDensity() (JS) and the mapHaze / uniMat fragment shaders (GPU) — the same formula three times over.
InhabitantsregionSpecies(), planetLore() in the lore layer; loreForBody() caches it on the live body.
LandmarksbuildSiteMesh(), updateSites(), sitePos() — pooled instances stood on the terrain normal.
Auto-landautoStep(), autoDescentRate(), autoWarpTarget(), and the 'auto' case in sasTarget().
Map levelssetMapLevel(), buildUniversePage(), buildSystemView(), makeMapPlanetMat().
Re-entrysystems() (thermal), plasmaMat, reentrySparks(), and the uHeat/uTint path in the composite pass.
WormholeopenWormhole(), updateWormhole(), whCore/whDisk/tunnel, and lensWarp() in the composite shader.
Ship & texturesbuildShip(), buildCockpit(), makeHullTextures() — all parametric, no assets.
GalaxyaddrSeed(), galaxyDensity(), systemsInVoxel(), generateSystem(), toPortal()/fromPortal(), loadSystem().
Galaxy mapbuildGalaxyPoints() samples the density field; nearestPoint() picks; warpToSystem() hands the address to the wormhole sequencer.
TouchTOUCH, bindStick(), bindThrottle(), applyTouchInput() — one control channel shared with the keyboard.

Known simplifications versus the full spec

  • Single star system; interstellar bridges are stubbed at the UI layer.
  • No vessel construction editor — the XR-7 is fixed.
  • Terrain geometry stops at ~2 m features; finer relief is fragment-shader normal detail only.
  • No scatter layer — the rocks/flora instancing described in section 4 is specified but not implemented here, so surfaces read as bare terrain up close.
  • Solar irradiance uses a compressed falloff rather than 1/r² (see section 10) so the outer system stays legible without auto-exposure.
  • Clouds are a single deck per body rather than a multi-layer weather simulation.
  • Shadows cover the vessel and its immediate surroundings, not terrain self-shadowing.
